bridge: C05 introduced executable inspection and D09 introduced evidence handling. Use only safe supplied artifacts; do not run an unknown binary.
teaching:
### Understand the memory snapshot

A memory image captures selected system memory at an acquisition point under a tool's method. It may contain processes, connections, loaded code and sensitive data. Acquisition can be incomplete or change the system itself.

Use analysis tools compatible with the operating system and image format. A failed interpretation can look like strange evidence when the real problem is the wrong assumptions.

### Separate static from running analysis

Static analysis examines a file without executing its program. It can reveal structure, imports and strings. Those clues do not prove every referenced action occurs.

Dynamic analysis observes execution in a deliberately isolated environment under explicit authority. This lesson does not require executing an unknown program; use the provided traces instead.

### Connect indicators with behaviour

A suspicious string or process name is a lead, not a complete malware diagnosis. Look for supporting operations and context. Record what was directly present and what you inferred.

### Protect the evidence

Memory can contain credentials and personal content. Restrict handling, avoid unnecessary copying into notes and preserve acquisition details. Report the exact scope of the supplied artifact rather than implying you examined an entire live system.
example:
Synthetic snapshot
PID 10: editor, parent 1, path /lab/editor, user A
PID 11: helper, parent 10, path /lab/helper, user A
PID 12: helper, parent 1, path /tmp/helper, user A
Connection: PID 12 -> docs.example at 09:05 UTC
Unknown: binary hashes, command lines, content, execution history
Observation only: PID 12 differs in path/lineage from PID 11.
explanation: The same name helper does not prove the same binary or intent. A /tmp path may justify further review, but the packet does not establish malicious activity. A snapshot also lacks some history: a process that terminated earlier may not appear.
exercise: Build a triage table for all three PIDs with observed facts, alternative explanations and next evidence requested. State preservation requirements and why process names alone are weak identifiers.
solution: PID 10: observed editor under A at /lab/editor, parent 1; plausible ordinary editor; request executable hash, provenance and command line. PID 11: helper under A at /lab/helper, parent 10; plausible editor helper; compare its hash/source and expected editor behaviour. PID 12: helper under A at /tmp/helper, parent 1, with a recorded connection to docs.example; possible temporary installer/helper or an unwanted process, with neither established. Request hash/provenance, command line, process start times, relevant logs and mapping/connection context. The same name does not establish the same binary, and PID numbers can be reused. Preserve the original snapshot and acquisition manifest, work on a copy and record tool/OS compatibility. Do not label PID 12 malware solely from this packet.
challenge: An analysis tool reports no PID 12 on an image from an unsupported OS build. Explain the limitation and propose a validation step before claiming the process never existed.
challenge_solution: Unsupported parsing invalidates that absence claim. Verify tool/image compatibility and collection integrity, compare supported independent evidence and report the analysis gap. A different snapshot time can also explain differing process lists.
